stories.title: India launches rescue operation as bulk carrier sinks off east coast
stories.summary: India's Coast Guard lost contact with the Panama-flagged cargo vessel Ocean Winner, which sank off India's east coast with 24 crew onboard. A rescue mission is ongoing, with two crew members already rescued from life rafts by Coast Guard vessels. The ship was carrying iron ore to Singapore and sank about 240 nautical miles from Paradip port; the cause of sinking is unknown. India’s maritime rescue agency on Aug 22 lost communication with Panama-flagged cargo vessel Ocean Winner, which sank off the coast of eastern India, the Indian Coast Guard said. The vessel had 24 crew on board, including 20 Chinese, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to Commandant Amit Uniyal, a spokesperson for the Indian Coast Guard. The Coast Guard sent two vessels for the search-and-rescue mission from Sri Vijaya Puram, formerly known as Port Blair, Uniyal said. The coast guard has rescued two people from life rafts. The search-and-rescue mission is under way for the seafarers on the vessel, the agency said. The Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore to Singapore after departing from India’s eastern Paradip port on Aug 20, according to government sources, adding that the ship sank around 240 nautical miles from the port. The cause of the sinking was not immediately known.

stories.title: How a new era of heatwaves could shake up the school calendar
stories.summary: Over the past two weeks, the sound of children has returned to Scotland's school playgrounds. Their summer breaks began in late June or early July and ended in mid-August. It's an academic year replicated in other European countries too. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, however, children will not return until early September. Their holidays are a similar length to Scotland's but England and Wales schools did not break up until late July, something that meant pupils were in school during the peak of the early summer heat. Or at least they were meant to be in school. While it was 30C or more outside, inside many classrooms it felt far hotter. With no air conditioning and limited ventilation, the heat became stifling and more than 1,000 schools across the UK either closed or sent pupils home early before the hottest part of the afternoon. Conditions were particularly challenging for GCSE and A‑level students sitting exams during extreme heat. Baroness Brown, chair of the UK's Climate Change Adaptation committee, has warned that "we know high temperatures can significantly impair concentration and performance" of children in schools. Back in February 2026, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said the timing of the school holidays should be reconsidered: "It's pretty hot usually in May, June and July, just at the point you're asking children to sit down and take an exam… so I think there is a need to have a good old look at it [the school year]." The recent hot weather has seen some parents join his call.
